utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I'm happy to see you again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, toward the end of yesterday's session shortly before we adjourned, we had been discussing - among other things - the differences in the potential traces left by permanent or fixed mortar positions and temporary mortar positions. I wanted to ask you if you were aware that at that time, because of the general situation, the VRS had instructed artillery and rocket units to fire from temporary positions in view of concerns about what NATO or Rapid Reaction Forces might do?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I could not possibly know about internal instructions of the VRS, but it's perfectly obvious that in any combat operation, any fixed position could be targeted. So it is inherent in artillery to regularly change combat positions, firing positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that respect, if I could call up a particular document, that would be 1D08009. Colonel, I'm not sure of your mastery of B/C/S and the extent to which I should read portions of this document to you in English so that you can understand it, but I'll do so for the record and for your potential benefit in any event. This is a document dated the 23rd of August, 1995, it's entitled: "Protection From Rapid Reaction Forces' Actions Order," delivered to all the SRK brigades and regiments. And it indicates, among other things, the following, that: "Due to the technical capability of the immediate discovering of the exact positions of active artillery rocket equipment and the actions of artillery rocket units and artillery pieces, it should be planned that temporary firing positions are to be used, which should be abandoned after the action." And then it goes on to have other instructions related to that order, and it's signed by Colonel Cedomir Sladoje. Colonel, I take it that this document is a reflection of what you mentioned before; that is, that one possible or likely reaction to the possibility of discovery would be to abandon fixed positions and adopt temporary firing positions for artillery and rocket units; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's perfectly right. This is a great document that corroborates my arguments. This order says that one should stay in one firing position the least possible time. So there would be no time to remove any traces of gunpowder or any fragments or any traces that would be left by the weapon. This document speaks eloquently in favour of what I have been saying so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, it's the case that these mortars, 120 mortar, for example, not to mention lighter mortars, can be set up and taken down in a matter of minutes; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, a mortar - mobile or fixed - can be easily set up and quickly made ready to fire. But it is one thing to just fix the base plate on the ground. Another thing is to set up artillery sites, to locate them according to landmarks, to prepare on the map the data that is necessary to know what charge to put inside at what angle. All that takes quite a lot of time, although of course not in terms of days, but it all depends on the operativeness and the readiness of the crew. But in any case the preparation of a mortar for firing takes 10, 20 minutes, and then the camouflage after the firing takes about half an hour or an hour, but usually nobody does that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was wondering how come it has been already noted as P5918.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There was a mistake on the part of the Registry. Yes, it will be admitted -- any objections, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted as P exhibit. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit P5918.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You are not tendering the document from angles and mils, albeit from Wikipedia, which you showed us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I -- yeah, that was an oversight. I would like to tender that, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't think we should sink to the level of admitting Wikipedia documents as exhibits. I think -- and the witness didn't confirm anything about it either, so I don't think there's a basis for admitting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in the current context of cross-examination I certainly have to disagree that a concept that reaches such a level of easy access and understanding plays a role in the cross-exam in this particular case I don't think it's necessary if it's going to generate an argument with the Court. I'm not overly concerned about this document, but I want to note as a matter of principle the argument raised by Mr. Robinson doesn't -- is not really apposite to points raised in cross-examination at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: No, but can't we just take as judicial notice the fact that NATO forces used 6.400 mils?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's another aspect as well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And everybody knows there's 360 degrees in a circle, so I mean we're not -- it's not rocket science, pardon the pun.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, which is part of the point that was made during the course of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And it's evidenced that Russians adopt the 6.000 mils system. If that's in record we don't have to admit that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As I say, Mr. President, I agree. I didn't want to create any unnecessary controversy over this particular document, so I'm fine with that resolution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any observation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. That resolution is satisfactory to us also. But I -- my point was basically that a Wikipedia document is not reliable enough to be admitted into evidence in principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd like to turn away for the moment from the question of an erroneous line of direction or the focus on an unduly narrow area from which it was considered the firing might have taken place. But instead, I want to focus now on the areas that you were looking at and referring to in the first place, that is, the -- your selection of the particular points --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. I object. This is testifying. When I made comments like this that suggests something that hasn't been said, the Prosecution objected. Look at this commentary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your objection, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection is that learned Mr. Tieger is commenting on something, that will be abandoned because things were so and so, he's testifying. He's suggesting something that has not the been established here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it he was referring to subject of his cross-examination, not necessarily the content of the evidence. Let's move on, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, as you indicated earlier and as was clear in the video that was shown, you based your calculations of the locations, that is, the distance the mortar would have travelled, from the relationship between the angle of descent and number of potential charges, as reflected in -- for a JNA 120-millimetre model M52; is that right? You show -- held up the firing table for an M52.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we used as one of the elements the table for that type of weapon and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tieger speak closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that. It's a little awkward in this courtroom, but I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were asked during the Dragomir Milosevic case whether you were aware that the VRS used an M74 millimetre mortar as well, that can be found at para 92, in fact, of your amalgamated witness statement. And you said at that time that the 120-millimetre mortars were produced by the Soviet Union and were in the arsenal of the entire former Yugoslavia, so it's one and the same system regardless of the particular model. Now, that didn't quite answer the question -- that's found by the way at para 92 of the amalgamated witness statement at transcript 8844 through 45. That didn't quite answer the question of whether you were aware, whether you knew at the time that the VRS had mortars other than the M52, so let me ask you that question now: Did you know whether there were mortars other than the M52 that might have been used in this particular instance?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to answer. 120-millimetre mortars do not have any modifications. It's one and the same mortar. If we are talking about calibre 122 millimetres, this is not a mortar it's a howitzer. It has nothing to do with mortars. It's a different type of weapon. This is a total confusion in the understanding of this document. Now, if we turn to K-54 or K-52 that we find in other documents or even 74, and in one document we see even 62, the shells differ across weapons systems, and of course mortars used -- use a range of shells that may not be very different between one another unless we include ballistic elements. That would be my answer. So I don't think this is a good understanding. There are no other mortars of this type. 122 millimetres is a howitzer, a different weapon used also by the weaponry. 120 was the one produced by the Soviet Union and exported into various other countries including Yugoslavia, and it has Russian-produced shells as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that's a lot of information not quite about my question. So let me ask it in a different way. Were you aware that the VRS had in its inventory not only an M52 mortar but an M70 120-millimeter mortar, but an M74 and an M75 among others, were you aware of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that practically all types of Soviet weapons were available to the Yugoslav army. Yes, I know that. The Yugoslav army did not have its own Yugoslav-produced weapons; they only had the Soviet ones. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You never heard of any Yugoslav arms industry that Yugoslavia produced, among other things -- I'm sure the accused would be happy to tell you a lot about that. He's very happy about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll abandon the question and move on, although I think it's something that's been -- we've already discussed in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before we move on, Mr. President, that was a comment for which you frequently rebuked Dr. Karadzic and I don't think it ought to go unnoticed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He said he would move on already, but I leave it at that. Let's carry on, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, you never heard of a Yugoslav arms industry producing such things -- such sophisticated weaponry, among others, as aircraft and APCs and other significant weaponry? You never heard of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And according to you, the -- Yugoslavia, former Yugoslavia, got everything from the Soviet Union and relied upon Soviet-produced weaponry only?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. I said that they had weapons including Soviet weapons. It's quite possible that they received weapons systems from other countries as well. I never said that they exclusively received it from Soviet Union. I did say, however, that what I came across in the VRS was typical standard Soviet weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In any event, based on your responses, it appears that you did not check any firing table for mortars in making your calculations other than the M52 firing table. You didn't check a firing table for an M74, you didn't check a firing table for an M75; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The principle that I followed was quite simple, to unmask the initial wrongly made conclusions. I started from what you saw on my sketch, a shell and then the mortar, et cetera. My task was to show that that was a lie. I had no other goal. It wasn't my objective to establish what actual weapon was used to fire the shell, et cetera, et cetera. That's the task for police, for ballistics expert, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, you assumed in the course of this exercise that the calculations that you obtained from the M52 firing table could be used to identify - as you told the Dragomir Milosevic case - the precise location from which the mortar -- the locations from which the mortar was potentially fired. That's the exercise you explained to us yesterday; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I investigated, the possible firing locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the assumption that all mortars were the same and that you could ignore any other -- either ignore or not be aware of any other mortars that could have been used and that might result in different firing distances, would have changed the potential locations from which they were fired; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. Let me remind you, several minutes ago you spoke about 122 mortar. There's no such mortar in the world --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I -- you're the one who mentioned 122-millimetre mortar, Colonel. Unless you got a different translation or unless I misspoke and didn't realise it, I don't believe I mentioned a 122-millimetre mortar. I certainly didn't intend to. So let's -- in any event, I had no intention of referring to a 122. If that's what you heard, and that's not what I either said or meant to say.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can certainly check that, but let's move on. The firing tables, mortar firing tables, and the shell that we assumed was used were the factors based on which it was concluded that a certain weapon was used to fire it. It was established by the Bosnian police and by the French ballistics expert. And then there was the information that we knew that the Serb forces around Sarajevo had in terms of weaponry. It would have been quite unusual if we were to assume that they had all of a sudden some new types of weapons and if our investigation was directed into that direction. The history simply taught us that that wasn't very likely. Now, as to the possibility of exploring today whether they had some kind of a secret mystical weapon that was possibly used to fire this shell, that would be groundless to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's first call up 65 ter 23850A. This is an inventory sheet as you can see from the heading of the weaponry that was distributed to units. As you can see it's an old inventory sheet used first by the JNA and then later by the VRS. It lists the weaponry of which the units are to report the quantities at the right, and it indicates - among others - the following weapons: an M -- 120-millimetre M52, 120 millimetre M75, 120-millimetre M74, and so on. Now, Colonel, you're not disputing that these weapons -- or are you disputing that these weapons were in the possession of the -- or in the inventory of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. I'm not disputing this. It's quite a clear list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't. I checked on that, Mr. President. I don't have the -- I don't have a date for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It says the document is from Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you please turn off your microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'll try to do that when I'm not using it. I was just about to.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P5919, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm just checking one thing on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, a moment ago you said that you used the firing tables and referred to the shell that we assumed was used in order to calculate the six possible locations of potential firing based on the six charges. Do you -- did you know at the time whether or not the M52 fired more than one shell?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about the details of the shelling except for the facts that I enumerated yesterday. Yesterday I said that in the sitrep that was issued on that day, on the 28th of August, they spoke of six instances of mortar shelling in town. So I compared the results of the explosions in that instance and other instances. Now, as to the specifics of that particular shelling, what mortar -- what shells were used in that instance, I'm not aware of that and I did not explore that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, if the M52 fired more than one shell, and if those two shells travelled different distances, then you would need to check out not six locations for six charges but 12 different locations for six charges for two different shells; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're absolutely right. I said yesterday, and I will repeat today, that in order to fully support the work of my commission I spoke of six possible locations. What we did in reality is that we drew on the map the entire territory where the mortars could have been placed and we explored 10, 20, 30, 40 possible locations, all the places where mortars could have been placed except in the forest, on the steep slope, and on the rocks. And we checked all of those locations. So regardless of whether there was one shell, two shells, whether there was one mortar or more, all of that was explored in the area that was accessible for a mortar to be placed there. And we didn't find any such locations. That was the essence of our investigation. We did not look for a single location. That would have been strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So that's your argument to the -- that's your position to the Court today. So in contrast to what you told the Dragomir Milosevic case about the precision of your locations, in contrast to what you told the media on September 2nd about how you went to six specific locations and made a determination; you now say that the particular locations were irrelevant because we went everywhere over thousands and thousands of metres and checked it out. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, that's not right. The six locations are very important. I never denied that. What I said is that in my interview and also in my testimony here five years ago, I emphasized the fact that, yes, those six locations were checked -- actually, not six but four. I mentioned several times in the interview and I mention nowadays, we did not check in principle -- possible locations on the Bosnian Serb side because our goal was to unmask a lie. So this was based on the firing tables. I can repeat once again that this was a broad exploration of all possible locations. I hope that I have answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those six locations and the four that you checked were based on the M52 firing tables but completely ignored whether or not the M52 fired two -- at least two different shells that travelled different distances. That's correct - isn't it? - because we're going to check the firing tables in just a second.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, yes, that's right. If we're going to check the firing tables, that's excellent, because if you're going to compare the firing tables with various modifications, 120 mortar and the shells used there, you will see that the differences are not great, not huge. And in principle, it makes no difference what shells were used. We checked everything. It makes no great difference between shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn then to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I warn that there was a possible mistake in translation page 13, line 13. The witness said that they -- out of those six possible locations, out of those six possible charges, in principle they did not explore the locations that were on the side of Bosnian Serbs. This is what is recorded that the witness said, but I believe that the witness said that, in fact, they did not check the possible locations on the side that was under the control of Bosnian forces. Could that be clarified with the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Otherwise I was about to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm ready to repeat. As you remember, in my interview I showed on the sketch six locations, so six charges, six locations. And you can see on that sketch the confrontation line as well. I spoke how it was possible that the fire could have been launched not only from the territory of Bosnian Serbs but also from the territory of the ABiH. However, we did not go there on purpose because it wasn't our goal to look for the culprits. There could have been there as well locations there that could have been possible firing locations, but it wasn't our task to explore there. Our task was to unmask a lie. So to look for the locations that were more elevated to the south was what our job was and I fully agree with this correction that is -- that was just made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, just by way of guidance I think in that situation you could have said that the clarification was correct and we could have moved on, but thank you for the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we call up 23864A, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a firing table for the M52 and it is the same firing table that you held up that is from 1972 as we can see on the video. Now, Colonel, as we can see on the -- on this page, this basic title page, the M52 uses a number of shells including the M49 and the M62; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn quickly to page 3 of the -- before going on to the calculations reflected by the number of charges, let me turn quickly to page 3 of the B/C/S and page 4 of the English. And there's a reference there to something that was discussed earlier, the change -- the time needed to change to a combat position, the time needed to change from a combat position. You see that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's reflected in the -- at the top half of the page time need -- under time needed for various aspects, change to combat position, change from a combat position, loading frontally from a combat position, loading onto a truck in pieces, and loading onto a truck folded, et cetera. But I'd now like to turn to the actual charging tables for both the M49 shell and the M62 shell. So if we could move forward on that and we've -- we'll try to present these as efficiently as possible and as clearly as possible for you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for that, Mr. President, in order to do that presentation as effectively as possible we need to go to Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We're first looking at charge 1 for an M49 shell. If you could show that on the -- and that's what the table reveals, 700 metres for - and we're looking to the right - for the angle of descent represented by 70 degrees. And that's in -- calculation using the number of mils; now charge 2, and that reflects 1200 metres, again for the figure that most closely approximates 70 degrees; charge 3, 1800 metres; charge 4, 2400 metres; charge 5, 3.000 metres; and charge 6, 3600 metres. Now if we could move on and take a look at whether or not the M62 shell, if used, travels different distances. So for charge 1 we see it -- that's 900 metres, so a 200-metre distance. For charge 2, 1600 metres. Charge 3, 2400 metres, now we've got a 600 metre difference. Charge 4, 3200 metres. Charge 5, 4.000 metres. Charge 6, 4700 metres. So the difference between the two shells at maximum charge of 6 is now 1100 metres, Colonel, which -- and I don't know what you meant when you said there was no difference, but there seems to be a difference of some significance reflected in this table. Now, were you -- I've already talked to you about M74s and M75s. Were you aware that the M74 and M75 also fired an M62 shell?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be some error in interpretation. Weapons cannot be used in a shell. Something is wrong. Maybe you mean shell for the weapon?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not sure how it was interpreted but the question is simply: Did you know at the time that the M74 also fired an M62 shell and also fired an M49 shell?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty, with accuracy, what other types of shell it was possible to use. But I want to say again, there's no need to enumerate all types of weapons or all types of ammunition that could have been used in that incident because, for instance, you have no basis for saying that an M62 mortar shell exploded. Show me, show me that that type of weapon was used. This is just an empty suggestion hanging in the air that something could have been used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Tieger, did you mean to say M74 or M52?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I'm moving on. We've just seen the tables for the M52, now I want to move on to the M74, and I asked the Colonel whether he was aware - before we looked at the tables for the M74 - what shells they fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, you've just said to me that I have no basis for saying that an M62 mortar shell exploded, but that's not the point, the point -- you're looking very happy about that, Colonel. But the point is that you had no basis for asserting that an M52 mortar was used, and you didn't even have any idea what shell was used - isn't that right? - in reaching your conclusions about firing locations?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking that's right because those few documents, those few reports based on which we acted, indicated a small area for the search, and our task was to conduct a more thorough investigation. At that point in time, to take into account dozens of different types of shells would have been odd. There was simply no basis for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we've already seen and discussed at considerable length - although I'd be happy to go back over it - what you said at the time, that is, during the media conference and what you said during the course of the Dragomir Milosevic case about what you were looking for and why. But you've also asserted today that there's no difference between these mortars and no huge difference in where the shells fired by those mortars are going to go if they used different shells. So that's what we're looking at right now. I'd like to turn to the M74 firing table, please. Here we see at charge --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, that is the -- that's 65 ter 23723A. And I'll also be turning to the M75 firing table which will be 23724A, so I just want to make clear so we can move through the presentation which contains all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At charge 1 for the M74, using an M49 shell, we see 8- to 900 metres; charge 2, 1400 to 1500; charge 3, 2100 to 2200; charge 4, 2800 to -- 2800; charge 5, 3500; charge 6, 4100. If we could now turn to the M62 shell: Charge 1, 1.000 to 1100 metres; charge 2, 1800 to 1900 metres; charge 3, 2700 to 2800 metres; charge 4, 3600; charge 5, 4400; charge 6, 5100? And finally if we can turn to the M75 table. Using an M62 shell: Charge 1, 1.000 metres to 1100 metres; charge 2, 1900 metres; charge 3, 2800 to 2900 metres; charge 4, 3700 metres; charge 5, 4500 metres; and charge 6, 5200 metres. So, Colonel, contrary to what you just told us a few moments ago that there would be no significant difference between which mortar was used and which shell was used in the distances travelled and therefore the potential firing locations, we can see here that there is a difference -- a potential difference of some between 3600 metres and 5200 metres, so a difference of some 1600 metres. Those are not the -- those -- the distances of the -- for the distances travelled are not at all the same for the different mortars that were potentially used or for the different shells. Isn't that right, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's perfectly right. But if you have evidence that fire was opened using that type of shell and that type of mortar resulting in different distances, you could operate on that, but you have no such facts. You are just theorising of what could have been. That's one. And two, when I said that there is no essential difference in the distance using different types of mortars and shells, I meant it made no difference to our investigating group. 2300, 2600, or 3.000 metres does not mean much when we are looking all over the ground, checking thousands of square metres of -- on that slope. And in our search for a place where a weapon, a mortar, could have been placed, it didn't matter really what distance the particular shell travelled. We checked everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The fact is, Colonel, you didn't know the distances travelled because you didn't know which mortars were potentially used. You didn't know that the M52 used different shells or how far they travelled. That was simply omitted from your exercise, and that's what you made clear when -- during your media conference and during your Milosevic testimony.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are trying to convince the Court that I'm not the greatest expert on the arsenal of the Yugoslav army, I will confirm. I did not serve in the Yugoslav army and I did not need to know the finer points of artillery fire of Yugoslav weapons and mortars. My task was different, to check the entire slope for any - and I underline any - trace of the positioning of such a mortar. The slope was checked, no trace of mortar was found and it doesn't matter if any different model was used or perhaps there was no different model. It doesn't make a difference. You also have no basis for talking about these shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We can argue about this a long time and I could turn your attention and the Court's attention back repeatedly to what was said earlier, but that doesn't -- that won't be necessary at the moment I think. Let me turn --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I would tender these documents, Mr. President, as well as the -- at least this final page for ease of reference for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you can print out this last page of this Sanction. So we'll admit this first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the last page will be Exhibit P5920.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll also admit the two further documents, 27823A as well as 23724A.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibits P5921 and P5922 respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Reid informs me that we didn't catch 65 ter 23864A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit that as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5923, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, I want to turn to the process -- just a little bit about the process through which you got into Bosnian Serb territory to look around at the -- at whatever sites you claim to have looked at. Did you seek authorisation or permission to go past the confrontation lines and to go into Bosnian Serb or VRS-held territory?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I did not have to ask anyone's position. My mandate as the Chief of Staff of the entire sector not only allowed me, it imposed upon me the duty to cross the front line on a daily basis because our task as peacekeeping forces was to inspect on one side as well as the other. That's one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, Colonel, that the VRS always scrupulously abided by the UNPROFOR mandate, and therefore the -- whatever your mandate was was never interfered with -- or whatever UNPROFOR's mandate was was never interfered with. Is that your suggestion to this Court?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, I can confirm numerous times that during my hundred, maybe even thousands trips across the check-points between the warring sides mean that I cross the front line many thousands times. If you want to ask in general whether the Bosnian Serb side violated the cease-fire agreement, then I will tell you that they certainly did and it was reported in various reports, including my reports. But if you're now inquiring about me personally and my team, I can tell you that I crossed the front line as often as necessary. And I didn't encounter many problems except for some manifestations of some attitudes, which is a separate topic for discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's set aside for the moment the question of how you personally were treated. Are you saying you were not aware of the fact that the Bosnian -- that the VRS restricted the movement of UNPROFOR personnel during the period of time you were there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please explain to me, restricted the movement of whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of UNPROFOR personnel.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say once again that you can find in documents in basically daily reports records of me crossing the front line numerous times. Perhaps you have some basis, some documents on the basis of which you are claiming that I was not allowed by the VRS to cross the front line, and if so please show me those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you're making a distinction which I explicitly asked you not to make in answering this question because I asked you a more general question which seemed to be implicated by your testimony. And that question is: Were you aware of restrictions of movement by the VRS of UNPROFOR personnel?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're speaking of. Are you implying that the UNPROFOR personnel was restricted in its movements or was it the VRS troops that were restricted in their movements or are you speaking of both?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm speaking about UNPROFOR trying to do what it was mandated to do and be prevented from doing so by the VRS, either because clearance requests were not granted or because they were granted but they were still not permitted to access certain territory or in any other way.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, in that case let me say both warring sides, the Bosnian army and the VRS, they both violated the agreement on the freedom of movement of the UNPROFOR personnel, both sides violated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you were also aware, were you not, that UNPROFOR would make clearance requests, requests for movement to particular positions in advance, and sometimes those were denied or rejected or refused or not complied with?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases, but as for me personally, I did not experience any restriction of my freedom of movement. And as I understand this examination today, you're now interested in my personal experiences not in the general situation during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me be clear with you, Colonel. I am also interested in the difference between how you were treated and how other UNPROFOR personnel were treated, and I'll be talking to you about that too. So we will be talking about both things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, shall we move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, that was particularly the case, that is, the concern about the movement of UNPROFOR personnel by August of 1995, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this does not pertain to me personally, if we're just speaking about the UNPROFOR freedom of movement, then yes there were difficulties throughout. Both warring sides limited the freedom of movement of UNPROFOR personnel; that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know why the VRS allowed you into their territory to conduct the exercise that we've been speaking about since yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm asking if you know why you were allowed into VRS-controlled territory to look for alleged or potential firing locations?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You posed the question incorrectly. You posed it as a statement, as though you're claiming -- you are claiming a Russian officer would be allowed to pass and others would not be allowed, which is not true. My rights and duties were identical to those of any other UNPROFOR officer. We had standard operating procedures whereby if we planned to visit, to tour, any sensitive points of one or the other side - sensitive in terms of their combat-readiness - then a request was to be made. It could have been made on the telephone, and we would receive an operative reply, yes or no, and also the dead-line for replying. There were no priorities and there was no preferential treatment granted to Colonel Demurenko, and I don't think you have facts claiming otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at D2284 and see what it was that the VRS itself considered in granting that request. This is a document issued by Chief Colonel Marko Lugonija sent from the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps Main Staff intelligence and security sector and it indicates the following. First a concern about potential -- or about NATO bombing or potential NATO bombing. And then information that they had that you disagreed with the assessment of UNPROFOR and requested permission from the VRS to personally visit the location which UNPROFOR assessed as the point from which the shell had been fired. And Colonel Lugonija proposes that you being given permission to do this after you mark the place that you will visit, and he also indicates that you had requested to visit hospitals in Blazuj where persons who were wounded in the shelling of August 28th were being treated. And Colonel Lugonija continues: "I propose to grant him permission for this too. Demurenko wants in this manner to persuade the UNPROFOR command that the Serbs did not fire the shell and that they were not the target."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the next page for English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Colonel, do you know who the source was who provided -- do you happen to know who the source was who provided this information that reached Colonel Lugonija about your request for permission?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I naturally do not know who the source was, but there were many of them. In the PTT headquarters of the UNPROFOR we had a number of liaison officers including those from the BSA. And since rumours spread quickly throughout the headquarters, for example, a rumour that I was not allowed to conduct a joint investigation -- joint additional investigation with UNPROFOR was something that the liaison officer immediately conveyed to his command, so it really makes no difference who conveyed what information. This was no secret. I never tried to conceal it. And thank you for showing this document. It confirms what I said about that there always was a request. Here you can see that Colonel Demurenko made a request to go to certain territory and this just confirms what I said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So this document is then accurate in its confirmation that you sought and received permission to go to particular areas?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it thus indicates that the -- so the VRS -- and that's why you were accompanied by a local commander when you went to those locations, right, local VRS commander who had been instructed by his higher command to accompany you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly. We cannot now go into the reasoning of the command of the 1st Romanija Corps. God knows what considerations they had and what they said to each other. But let me repeat once again, this perfectly shows what I said earlier. A request was made, a reply was received, it was determined at what time it would be implemented, with whom, and a military guide was made available who assisted us in orientating ourselves and going to the location. This is a standard procedure; it applied not only to the Russians but to everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now I indicated --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That document is already in evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is one of the associated exhibits which Colonel refers to in his statement in para 135.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you raised the -- actually, we both mentioned the treatment of you in particular by the VRS. I want to confirm, first of all, that when you refer to your team that the core group of the team, that you relied on in this exercise, consisted of fellow Russian officers; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were Russian colleagues, yes. As for any privileges, no, I did not have any preferential treatment. I received the same treatment as everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions then about the general, and then more specific, relationship between Russians serving in UNPROFOR and the Bosnian Serbs or the Serbs generally. First of all, you recall our earlier reference to the Komsomolskaya Pravda interview in 1996, and there you noted that Serbs and Russians were brought together by history and that Serbs are a people whom Russians consider dear. Is that a sentiment you still agree with?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be odd to deny that. That's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And would you consider that to be part of the basis for your reaction to allegations concerning the actions of the VRS and the Bosnian Serbs or at least the level of emotion with which you reacted to such allegations?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. Not at all. As you know, I was a high-ranking officer. I understood perfectly well the requirements of both military science and the UN theory about impartiality. I simply don't have time, but I could tell the Court dozens of cases and perhaps hundreds of cases when I, on the contrary, tried to establish the truth concerning the suffering of Bosnian Muslims in this city of Sarajevo under blockade. They suffered in all possible ways, and I found it strange when my colleagues at the staff smiled at me, or rather, smirked, saying, "You are a Russian. Why are you defending Muslims?" And I said always, "I'm not a Russian here. I am a peacekeeper and I do care about blood being shed, never mind whose blood." I'm sorry I can't find it - in my archives, perhaps, my personal notes - all these anecdotes about cases when I defended Muslims. As for the closeness between the Serbs and the Russians, that's impossible to deny. That's history. And my personal involvement in that incident has nothing to do with it. My point was to prove that we should not be taken for fools who will always listen to the command and nod. We needed to expose the truth and that's what I set out to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But let me ask you about a more concrete example then, and in particular one you were asked about during the Dragomir Milosevic case. And there were some questions then about whether your nationality and being from Russia and the Russian-Serb closeness had an effect on what you thought or did. And as part of that you were asked whether it was true that Russians got preferred treatment because they were not taken prisoners in May when "all the other UNPROFOR or other UNPROFOR members were taken prisoners." That's found at 8972 of the Dragomir Milosevic transcript. You responded that the Russian station in Gorazde were not captured because they were on territory controlled by the SRK and that would create some tactical issues involving the risk of losses. That's at the same page, 8972. But setting aside the situation of the Russian personnel in Gorazde, are you asserting that Russian personnel were not treated differently during the period when UN personnel were being taken captive from similarly situated fellow UNPROFOR personnel?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can answer that. It's a very large and interesting topic for further inquiry, the emotional -- the influence of emotional factors of international personnel in their relationship with local population. But there was more sympathy or even neutrality towards Russians, that's true, but that was not strange. Let me tell you about our peacekeeping battalion in one of those areas. It was never attacked or taken captive by Bosnian Muslims; on the contrary - and it's in the sitrep - our soldiers were injured many times by shells falling from Grbavica, from Serb-controlled territory. Why that happened is a separate issue. But it was not an individual case. It was not all love and friendship, far from that. War is war and there was equal danger to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So can you tell us why you didn't simply tell the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber when you were asked about this issue that, yes, in fact Russians did receive different treatment from the VRS during the course of the taking of captives -- about taking UNPROFOR personnel captive?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over these two days I come across again a question that invokes a hypothetical question, hypothetical situation. Why didn't you say, you ask me? There are many things in my life that I didn't say, didn't answer, didn't warn people against. There was no chance and no time to answer all this. I have to say again I'm not taking back anything I said in previous times, including the Milosevic trial. I am standing by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to make clear, the question is not why you didn't volunteer it during the course of your testimony. The question is: Why, when asked specifically whether that happened, you simply directed the -- your answer to the -- you simply said basically because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I think the witness has answered the question. Shall we move on -- but I note the time. But for planning purposes, can I know how much longer you would need to complete your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I estimate about a half-hour, Mr. President. I hope that's accurate, but it's certainly roughly accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me just clarify one thing before we move on any further, Colonel, and that's in relation to some of the issues discussed yesterday rather than today. First, is it correct that you do not consider yourself an expert on anti-terrorism?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that you do not consider yourself an expert on static explosions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, is it also correct that you do not consider yourself an expert in crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we were talking about UNPROFOR personnel taken captive in May and June of 1995 and that's a subject you discussed to some extent in your amalgamated witness statement at paragraphs 70, 73, and 76, stating that it was an adequate response from the Bosnian Serbs to respond in this way - that's at paragraph 70; that the use of the term "hostage" was not really proper but was used because UNPROFOR couldn't come up with a proper word - that's at paragraph 73; and at paragraph 76 that they were not real hostages. Colonel, were you aware that UN personnel taken captive were threatened with death by the VRS or Bosnian Serbs if the UN either failed to do something or -- that was demanded or was unwilling to refrain from doing something or that UN personnel were placed in locations as human shields to inhibit any bombing of those places as potential targets? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that. Also, it's true of the other warring party. I have heard of such cases involving the BSA, although I was not an eye-witness and I didn't hear it with my own ears, but in the case when Bosnian Muslims captured a UN post manned by Russian soldiers, my soldiers told me that they were threatened with death when they were taken prisoner. Coming back to your question, there have been such cases and it would be odd to deny it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, probably you referred to the old para numbers in the 92 ter statement. In the meantime, could you check it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, I meant pages, not -- those are not designated by paragraphs. That was my mistake. So if you substitute "pages" for "paragraphs," I think it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, you discussed an incident that you asserted took place at -- you discussed was what you called the only incident between Serb forces and UNPROFOR after the NATO bombing, and that was what you said to be the fighting at the brotherhood and unity bridge. That's at your amalgamated witness statement at paragraph 38. Would it refresh your recollection about where that incident took place if I told you that the only incident that took place between Serb forces and UNPROFOR after the NATO bombing was -- took place at the Vrbanja bridge. Is that the -- was that the incident you were discussing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I don't remember if the brotherhood unity bridge is the same as Vrbanja bridge or it's a different bridge. I simply don't remember. But I remember that on the brotherhood and unity bridge there was a lot of bloodshed in a mutual attack when many UNPROFOR soldiers, French soldiers, were killed, and there must have been other cases. I do remember. They did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'll turn your attention to some documents about the incident, but first let me remind you of how you characterised it in your amalgamated witness statement. And that was essentially that there were two check-points at either end of the bridge with Serbs and Muslims shooting at each other, Serbs went on the offensive and captured the Muslim trenches, so the Muslims told the French about this and the French command ordered its French troops to attack the Serb units at the check-point. So that was your characterisation of the incident, and I take it in your -- that was your -- you were citing that as an example of UNPROFOR siding with Muslims against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't look at it so narrowly, that it was typical of UNPROFOR in all ways, in all cases, to take the side of Muslims. But in that particular case it was quite an atypical involvement of UNPROFOR into combat. From the very beginning in many documents and briefings and training sessions, it was said to UNPROFOR soldiers that they should not use weapons except for self-defence or, if necessary, to stop bloodshed between the warring parties, the so-called peace enforcement. And I'm recalling that case more because it was an exception rather than the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in contrast to your characterisation of how this happened, let me turn your attention to P2171. It's a cable concerning that incident as we look at -- scroll down the page and look at point number 4 concerning UN observation points in Sarajevo. And it refers to nine French soldiers detained at the observation point and a further ten disarmed and detained, and relates that at 0430 hours that morning a group of the Bosnian Serb army dressed in French UN uniforms and equipment took over the FreBat 4 OP at Vrbanja bridge in Sarajevo and removed 10 French soldiers. And it continue that 0800 FreBat 4 mounted a successful operation to regain control of the OP and that soldiers were killed on both sides. So, in fact, Colonel, it was not the case that the Muslims ran to UNPROFOR after their position was captured and then UNPROFOR went on the attack on their behalf. It was the case that the Bosnian Serbs attacked the French observation post wearing French uniforms and then the French Battalion retook the position. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not right. You took as evidence a report from the superior command as I understand, a report by General Janvier to the UN. Why don't you take a sitrep that speaks to the same incident in Sector Sarajevo where it happened and compare the information in one report and in the other. As you understand, on the ground things are much clearer than up at the top, and then you would see what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's do that, Colonel. Let's turn to 65 ter 23897. And this is a document that was signed off on by you. So we look at the first page, we see there was a confrontation between BSA and UNPROFOR with reconquest of the Vrbanja OP east. We see at the bottom of that paragraph "all disarmed personnel Bosnian Serb army keeps as hostages." If we turn to page 4, "The hottest point was the reconquest by FreBat 4 of the Vrbanja bridge OP seized by treachery during the last night by Bosnian Serb Army dressed like UNPROFOR personnel with dead, wounded, and captured personnel on both sides." If we turn to page 7, "FreBat 4 at -- on the 27th at 0400, Bosnian Serb Army soldiers invade the Vrbanja bridge OP dressed with UN equipment. Between 0800 and 0900 a platoon of FreBat 4 reconquered the OP," with exception of the OP western of the position, and it relates that personnel were killed. If we go on to page 10 and 11 we see similar reports. Toward the bottom of the page, reports that today at 0430 Bosnian Serb army soldiers who were wearing in the UN French clothes uniform, helmet, flak jackets, seized Vrbanja bridge and blocked 12 times French UN soldiers in the OP. And then on the next page we see references to the recovery. And if we -- and on page 13 we see a reference to the Bosnian Serb army considering UN soldiers as shields. So not only was the previous document we looked at an accurate representation of what happened, Colonel, but you knew about it at the time. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be advantageous for me to use your methods when you compared the figures, the figures that I mentioned and the figures that you had in your hands. If we were to have a bit more time, which we don't have, and if we were to look at the first report where it said 4.30 in the morning, nine soldiers, ten soldiers, and then they mention the uniform of the special forces of the French army, whereas in this document they mention the UN uniforms, not the French uniforms. So there's a lot of contradiction in these three reports. This is just another indication of the manipulation that took place. Depending on who signed the report, they twisted the truth, they twisted the reality, put their spin on it. So in all these three documents that you showed, the time, the participants, the uniforms, all of that is described differently. That means that one could play it any way one wanted, relying on each of these reports individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to introduce this document into evidence, Colonel, and we'll let the Chamber make the comparison between the documents, what they reveal, what you knew at the time, and what you said in your amalgamated witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have no objection, Mr. President, but we would appreciate the avoidance of comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is for the Chamber to assess the evidence at the end of the trial. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5924, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, you said in your amalgamated witness statement at paragraph 9 that you never met with Mladic -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- or other leaders while you were Chief of Staff. I think your quote was: "In Sarajevo sector I practically had no dealings with the leadership of the warring parties." And you went on to note that that approach was in support of your duty of impartiality, and therefore you only had contact with liaison officers. I wasn't quite clear on what that meant, when it meant to say, "I practically had no dealings with the leadership of the warring parties." Did that mean you never met with them or that you had limited contact with them or that in a practical sense -- what did that mean?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a good comment, a useful comment. What I meant to say when I said that I practically never met them meant that we didn't meet individually or for a special reason, but naturally it was my duty, in view of my rank and my position, to meet with the warring sides and with their senior leadership. I met Mladic several times as part of an official delegation, and I also met the general whose name I cannot remember now who was on the side of the Bosnian Muslims in Sarajevo, commander of the corps there. Yes, that was part of my regular duties and I met with them in that capacity, but other than that we did not have any private or behind-the-scenes meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what would -- what were the subjects raised or discussed or addressed at these meetings with Mladic when you were part of an official delegation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we met and when I was part of an official delegation, there was almost invariably just one issue raised which was how to ensure that, in this particular case the Serb side, would abide by its duties pursuant to a cease-fire agreement or to the disarming agreement or withdrawal of heavy weaponry agreement. Those were the kinds of issues that we discussed. Perhaps I am running ahead of myself. I heard rumours that you may have a document about my alleged attempts to meet with Mladic individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when did you hear those rumours?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came across that in the documents that I have, the documents that were shown to me by a representative of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So why is it a -- why would that be a rumour if you saw a particular document and what document are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it in the Defence material. There was a letter there by one of the staff officers which mentions that, my request to meet with General Mladic. I could not have seen that document earlier because it was an internal document of the Bosnian Serb army, but during proofing when I worked with the representatives of Defence I was shown that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what were you -- what did the letter -- what were you trying to meet with General Mladic about when that letter was sent?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will need a bit more time to explain. I'm now refreshing my memories of that period. If you remember, the format of the peacekeeping operation at that time changed. There were broader agreements on cease-fire assigned, the US army got actively involved in September -- and then in October when I returned back from Moscow following my short annual leave and some business that I needed to attend to there, I returned back and I was the only one at the time - and to this day I'm still the only Russian officer with American education and training. So I had discussions at the Ministry of Defence on how could we, together with the US army, establish a new group, a new working group on co-operation within the UN and perhaps not just the UN but more within the framework of NATO. And if you remember, it was implemented. We set up a US -- or rather, a Russian Brigade. We established a US-Russian sector. We removed our battalion from Grbavica. And in the early days of those events I was instructed to have consultations with both sides, the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Muslims and, if necessary, the Croats as well, as to what the format would be, what the tasks would be, and where that plan would be implemented. So this was my task for the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you also talk to General Mladic about the possible provision of personnel, Russian personnel, or weapons to the VRS or to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me start by saying that in the end I did not meet with General Mladic. I asked to meet; however, we did not meet subsequently. So it all remained on paper, in the planning phase. It was not implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn to P1489, page 108, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As this is coming up, Colonel, let me tell you that this is a copy of General Mladic's notebook. And here we see, as we get to one -- this page, that on the 21st of October, 1995, at 1700 hours there was a meeting with General Mladic, General Tolimir, Colonel Salapura, Major Bukva, and you, Colonel Demurenko, and it goes on to discuss the items, to identify the items discussed, which include as we scroll down to page 21 -- I'm sorry, paginated page 21. That will be two pages ahead from 108, I guess 110 in the e-court. Sorry, just go one page back, please. Goes on to discuss "the possibility of dispatching special troops of the Russian army to the Main Staff. We are prepared to dispatch them immediately. We would like to know how many, when, and what groups to dispatch. Initially it can be a symbolic group but that could be increased." And then it goes on to discuss the possible provision of weapons. "... there we can opt for weapons through the company and in the future ..." Turn the page, please. To go through the "... Russian contingent or through third countries." And it goes on to discuss the use of a private, not state-run, company and so on. Isn't this in fact a reflection of a meeting that you just told us didn't take place, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you remember, I first spoke about discussing with General Mladic individually the format of the future peacekeeping operation. And as you can see none of that is mentioned in this document, this future peacekeeping operation. This involves two completely different events that have nothing to do with each other. As I have told you, concerning the first issue, I was never given an opportunity to meet with Mladic. As for this meeting here, yes, it did take place. It was an official visit, official delegation, we officially discussed the plans that the Russian side had and that the Republika Srpska had. In this meeting I was present as a member of delegation, I did not head the delegation, and we simply exchanged information as is typical for peacekeeping forces as to what difficulties we encountered and so on. Nothing more than that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also discussed some of your -- you also raised the issue of some of your discussions with General Mladic and your opinion of General Mladic during the course of that Komsomolskaya Pravda article we referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to that, please, and that is 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Colonel, I wanted to leave it there but I couldn't. You just said that you did not head the delegation, but could we see the page two pages ahead, 108. It clearly says Mladic said it was a meeting with you, nobody else, but Tolimir, Salapura, and Bukva from the VRS. Could you clarify that, Mr. Demurenko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain. I'm mentioned here as a military representative, senior one. But as for all the people who went to Banja Luka, there were also non-military personnel there present representing the interests of the Russian Federation. They were there in order to have consultations and to participate in negotiations. That was their role there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Back to you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just called up 65 ter 23846.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in the course of that interview, Colonel, you also referred to the fact that you had occasion to meet with Serb leaders. And you said it would be difficult to find a better commander - and that can be found, by the way, in the second column if we scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Scroll down in the Russian, please, for the benefit of the Colonel, and I think you'll find that at about -- scroll do you happen a little farther, please. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you see where that bar is to the right side of the page with the little insert, if you look immediately to the left of that in the second column and the first paragraph below that, that's the portion I'm referring to where you explain that you had occasion to meet with the Serb leaders and it would be difficult to find a better commander than General Mladic, and you describe him as extremely talented, exceptionally literate, tough commander, and then go on to describe some difficult conversations that the two of you had in which he accused all of Russia betrayal. Did those conversations take place in the meetings you described earlier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it is on page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I'm sorry, Mr. President, I should have alerted the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, I'm not really prepared to speak of chronology, what happened first, what happened later. And at any rate, I do not take back anything I have uttered. I stand by what I said. Simply, I think that things should not be taken out of context. As you know, when you take something out of context you twist the original meaning. If I spoke about General Mladic being a talented commander, then there was a reason for that. He had graduated from three military academies, magna cum laude. He was awarded a gold medal for each of those diplomas. He took military decisions that did not lead to mass bloodshed. So if you were to quote me as saying that everybody betrayed them, that is not true. It's possible that I was perhaps disappointed by the official position taken by the Russian Federation, which distanced itself from taking part in the international conflict and simply observed things from the sidelines. So I could give you a number of facts to support this position of mine. They simply, for example, forgot about me, their colonel. They simply forgot about me in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They never called me on the phone, they never wrote to me, they never invited me for meetings with persons who should be interested in what I knew. But it's okay that they treated me that way. I'm just an ordinary soldier. Simply, Russia was lost and intimidated at the time and didn't know which position to take. Those sentiments of mine are reflected in this article and to this day I still believe what I said back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The last subject I want to turn to, Colonel, concerns some references that you made in your amalgamated witness statement at approximately page 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you not tendering this --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- interview at --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5925, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At page 70 you refer to a sitrep that was originally 1D28149, I don't have the exhibit number at the moment. And you indicate -- the sitrep indicates that mortar and artillery, including homemade bombs, fire also will continue in the usual hot areas, and then you commented that both sides used the homemade bombs. I wanted to turn your attention, Colonel, to 1D28167 -- if someone could call up -- I'm sure that's in evidence too. I don't have the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2318, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. And if we could scroll down the page a bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, that refers to - and this is again a document signed off by you that was a part of your amalgamated witness statement - it refers to one more big explosion detonated since last month in the vicinity of the TV building killing one Bosnian civilian and injuring another four. According to the outcome of investigation, it was a suspected homemade rocket consisting of a shell body and four times small rocket propulsion devices. Origin is still unknown. Is that another reference to the homemade bombs that you referred to in the document we just looked at and at page 70?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that yet -- is that just another reference to the homemade bombs you were referring to at page 70 of your amalgamated witness statement?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. There is no contradiction. It's just a repetition, a repeated reference to one and the same facts or similar facts. If you want me to elaborate on the homemade bombs, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine. I think I used the time I suggested to the Chamber. I would and -- thank you for your time, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That concludes my examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies. I have a few questions. Good morning, Your Excellency. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel. Yesterday Mr. Tieger on transcript page 6970 suggested that the line of direction that you toured -- sorry, pages 69 and 70, that the axis that you toured in the direction 170 degrees plus/minus 5 was a result of the fact that you applied Russian parameters to Western systems. Do you remember saying that? And that's why your calculation was faulty.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember what I said. I remember everything I said. I confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see P150 or 65 ter 10415 in e-court, please. Can we now see page 3 in this document. We can remove the Serb version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who made this -- did you make this report or did someone else?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I suppose it was somebody from the UNPROFOR headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, if I may draw your attention to the first line which includes various elements, time, position, and the bearing 170 plus/minus 5, this was not done by you. You received it from the UN; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 1 to see whose report this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whose report this is?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the signature, it's Colonel Konings and somebody, Captain Carbonna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So did you determine the direction yourself or did you get it from them?
