utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said already, my first documents indicating the direction and the angle of descent we received from those who did the first investigative steps, and then we took it from there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 65 ter 9912 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, please, look at this document, tell us who drafted it and what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we can do without the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who is sending this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Scroll down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see that, General Janvier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The passage referring to Sector Sarajevo, can you please look at it. I should now like to read beginning with line 5. "This mortar shell was assessed to be fired from 100 [as interpreted] degrees magnetic [in English] in investigation to determine the distance to the firing point is ongoing."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I think there was a misinterpretation. Instead of 100 degrees that was interpreted, it should have been interpreted 170 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the case that the UN's position was that it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Objection --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- that it was 170 degrees --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Objection, objection. I'm sorry to interrupt but I knew I'd have to start this early. Even in re-direct, the accused is going to have to refrain from leading questions, which I think is starting to be a habit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best, Your Excellencies, but for two years I had the right to ask leading questions and now I have to get used to not being able to anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in view of these few sentences I read out, can you tell us what was the position, the official UN position, concerning the direction from which this shell arrived?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously it was not different from the one I arrived at in my investigation, 170 degrees. There are no other variants here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see P1446, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the UNMO daily sitrep.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 21.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 2 -- sorry, the third paragraph. What was the position of the UNMO, the military observers, concerning the direction from which the shell arrived?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's obvious. It's again 170 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I now ask for P1444.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To shorten this without leading, I'm reading here that this is an UNMO HQ daily sitrep dated 30th August 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see page 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the first line in the last paragraph "PTL investigated," and in the second line can you tell us what was the position of UN military observers on the 30th of August regarding the direction from which the shell arrived?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we go through these points one by one, after the words "the Federation side" and we see the bullet points, we see again in the second bullet point 100 degrees again if I'm saying this well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 170 degrees --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 170 degrees, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, did you use any map when you went out to -- in the field to inspect possible positions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. Military men do not move around without a map. A map was the basis for us finding our way on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the direction of approach of the shell marked on that map and was the margin of error accounted for with regard to the range?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, apparently Mr. Karadzic is seeking guidance in the questions, so how about a question: What was on the map? Rather than specifying what he would like to see on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. This sounds like advocacy training. But could you reformulate the question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I'd like to thank Mr. Tieger too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, what could be seen on the map?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A map is the main document for the military. One can find everything on the map. So in that particular case we took an empty, a clear, map and then drew the direction line, the likely direction from the crater to the firing position. And then on that direction line we marked the possible firing positions, relying on the six or four possible charges. And then on the map I tasked my team to check the entire area. In the video excerpt you could see that the majority of the terrain in that area is covered by a forest. There's less than 30 per cent of the territory that's clear. As you know, mortars cannot fire from forests. And as I have said, I directed my team to explore, investigate, the entire area shown on the map except for forests, and that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 123 of your statement, page 56, you say that all directions under 170 degrees, plus or minus a few degrees, weren't suitable for mortar positions because they were steep and there was a lot of brushwood there - is that what it says? - there was a lot of growth. It was very rocky. Is that what it says? Is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that also concern an angle of 160 degrees?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would also apply to the other line that I showed in that video excerpt. We did not only explore the 170 angle plus/minus 5. We explored much more than that starting from 160 and then onwards. It wasn't very difficult to do that because there were very few flat and open areas, meadows. So it wasn't difficult for us to tour all of them, take photographs, and explore them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 51 of your statement, page 20, you said that your investigation took three days. How much time did you spend in the field and how much time did you need to reach your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least one and a half full days was spent walking throughout that area. Then we needed several hours to put everything on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of your examination today, page 1 of the transcript, my learned friend Mr. Tieger suggested that units from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps transferred the artillery to other positions because there was the danger of NATO bombing, and you were shown document P10918 that was signed by Colonel Sladoje. P918 is the number. Now I would like to show you two documents -- P5918. P and the number 5 in the Serbian language sound similar. I would now like to show you D1013. D1013. It's a short document. I hope we'll be able to deal with it rapidly. This is also a document signed by Mr. Sladoje addressed to all the brigades. I'll read it out. "I caution again all unit commanders about my order on banning opening fire on the city of Sarajevo without a pre-approval from the corps command post." Under 2: "You are to inform the corps command in writing by 1400 hours about whether you have opened fire between 1000 and 1200 hours on the town of Sarajevo. If you have, inform us of the time when this was done, the target, and the calibre and weapons used, as well as the reasons for which this was done. The report is to be submitted for artillery weapons of calibre 80 millimetres and above." Thank you. Before I put my question to you I would like us to have another look at another document, 65 ter 16583. This is also from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. It's to the president of the Republika and to corps commands. Could we please have a look at page 3 now and it's page 4 and then 5 in the English version. This part of the combat report has to do with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, concerns the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Third page in the Serbian language and I'll read it out now. It's page 5 in the English version. I'll read out the part at the top. "Commanders of the 1st, 2nd, and 4th Sarajevo [as interpreted] infantry brigade, the Igman and the Ilidza Brigade, and the mixed artillery regiment, confirmed the corps command in writing that they did not fire artillery weapons on the city of Sarajevo between 1000 and 1200 hours on the 28th of August." When you were conducting your investigation in Serbian territory, did anyone from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps inform you that the Army of Republika Srpska had conducted such an internal investigation into whether anyone from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had opened fire?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anything about this. Moreover, what I did showed my principled attitude, which is to go beyond the two sides and to conduct an impartial investigation, that is, to show the truth. I didn't ask one side or the other side on purpose. I didn't inquire with them whether they opened fire. The task of peacekeeping forces is to be neutral and to conduct a neutral investigation and to produce conclusions. Had the conclusion been different, I would also announce it. But the conclusion was the one I reached and I had no knowledge of this document and the similar material. I see it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to the results of this internal investigation, do these results correspond to the findings that you obtained in the field?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be admitted, the last one wasn't admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have no doubt there are plenty of opportunities to tender this document, but this didn't -- it's not a subject that arose from cross-examination which was about -- I see the Court nodding so I won't explain further. And I don't think this kind of generic comment about the document would in any event be sufficient in this instance for admission, so I imagine there -- as the Court is -- want to say, there will be a number of opportunities to do so. I don't think that this is the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wondered how it is related to the document we see during the cross-examination which is related to the protection from Rapid Reaction Force. I'll discuss with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Tieger. You have another opportunity to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 29 of today's transcript it was suggested to you that Russian members of UNPROFOR were not captured by the Army of Republika Srpska in May and June 1995. My question is as follows: Did Russia participate in the bombing of Republika Srpska in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you hear the question, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did hear, but I'm sorry, I'm not following. What do you mean "participated"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The forces from various nations participated in bombing under NATO. Were Russian planes involved in the bombing of Republika Srpska? Did they take part in that bombing? Did they participate in it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even though we were already members of the partnership for peace and NATO, we were not full members of NATO and are not likely to become, so we absolutely did not take part in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, for having come here to testify.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. "Spasibo," Colonel, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of this Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say something. I'm very grateful to this high Court, to everybody here, including the Prosecution, for their impartial analysis and their attempts in sorting out difficult questions and in your patience for hearing me out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the time, it's better to take a break now. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's fine as long as you don't charge it to our account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll break till ten past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.20 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Very quickly, one housekeeping matter. For the 65 ter in e-court for the last slide of the presentation that was admitted as P5920, the 65 ter number should be 23922 for the benefit of the Registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D4831 in the e-court system for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you have it before you, is this your statement, and have you had the opportunity of seeing a hard copy of your statement, of going through it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: This looks like the statement which I have written and signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we show him the entire statement, next page, and one page by one page. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my statement. This is my signature. There was one correction which I notified to both sides to one of the paragraphs, it's about the location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Apart from that correction, does this statement fully and accurately reflect what you, in fact, said?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I put the same questions to you today, would your answers be the same as those provided in the statement?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yes, with the exception of the correction needed in paragraph I think it's 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to that and we'll make the necessary correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, could this statement please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Any objection, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D2329.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out a brief summary of the statement. In order to proceed efficiently, I will read it out in English. [In English] Paul Conway was an officer of the Irish army who served at the United Nations military observers in the former Yugoslavia from July 1995 through July 1996. He arrived in Sarajevo in early August 1995. He is now retired from the military and since 2001 has held the civilian post as superintendent of the Irish parliament in Dublin. On 28th of August, 1995, at about 9.00 a.m., Commandant Conway arrived at the United Nations observation post known as OP 1 with Thomas Knustad and an interpreter. At around 11.00 a.m. he heard the sound of several explosions. The sound was muffled. A few minutes later he was contacted by UNMO headquarter and asked if he had seen anything. He immediately went to the observation post where he saw plumes of smoke coming from the market area in the city. He is unable to state whether the explosions he heard were from outgoing or incoming fire. In December 1995 he came across a Bosnian army mortar position south of Sarajevo. There were at least four mortars pointed north toward the city of Sarajevo. The mortar position appeared to be well-established and to have existed for a considerable period of time. Prosecution witness Thomas Knustad marked on the map the location of OP 1, the location of the confrontation line, and the direction of fire of the shell which landed on the market -- Markale market on 28th of August, 1995. This map was admitted as Prosecution Exhibit P151. Commandant Conway has marked on this map the approximate location of where he found the Bosnian army mortar position. This location is in the direction in which it is alleged that the shell had landed -- that landed in the Markale market had come from. The map marked by Commander Conway has been given another e-court number 1D4832, and I would ask to see it in the electronic court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this map was obtained by the Prosecution from Thomas Knustad and did you add anything to this map; if so, what did you add and what sort of markings have you made on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in, please. [In English] Did you get my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay, sorry, I wasn't sure if I was expected to respond. There is a marking on the map which says the estimated position of mortars alongside the road which runs parallel to river, I made that marking, that's my marking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would first like to ask you whether OP 1 has been marked at a location in area that was under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: OP 1 was within the Bosnian army area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you said that it could have been between 3 and 4 kilometres from the Markale market; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: That's what I said and I measured it since on a more accurate map. I think 4 kilometres is probably further than I had imagined. I think 3 is probably closer or more accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far towards the south from the OP 1 position was the Muslim line in fact located?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: About 2- 300 metres. OP 1 was on a steep slope and the confrontation line was behind the OP. It was at approximately 300 metres. I never walked the distance through the confrontation line. I just knew it from the map marking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the Serb line, the Serb trenches, where were they in relation to the Muslim lines? Were they even further away; and if so, what sort of distance are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: I never visited the Serb positions which were to the south of OP 1. I only observed them closer down to the river in the French Battalion area where the confrontation lines were very close. But in the area of OP 1 I never observed the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have marked a position where there were at least four mortars of the ABiH. Was it possible to detect those mortars at an earlier date? Were there any restrictions on UNPROFOR members visiting those places?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: No, it was not possible to go into that immediate area. There is a road that runs parallel to the river south of the river and there were check-points on both ends and we had never been given freedom of movement down that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were at OP 1, did you ever observe mortar shells that were fired from the south on the town, not only on the 28th but at any time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: In my personal time on OP 1, I did not observe any other mortar fire instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any of your predecessors or of your colleagues inform you that shells were fired over the OP position from the south and on the town and in the direction that has been marked here?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, as to the form.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the question was: Did anyone inform you of the existence of such fire if you personally did not observe any such incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, no. There were mortar instance to the east of the market position in the Egyptian Battalion area, but I did not investigate those occurrences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 18 you made a correction. The word "northern" was changed and it now reads "southern ." Isn't that correct? Is that in fact the correction that you made?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The map marked by the witness will be admitted as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D4832 will be Exhibit D2330.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Conway.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I understand your role as a military observer to be one of impartiality; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And why was impartiality so important?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: It was essential that any information that was given was accurate as well as impartial. It was being relayed back to UN headquarters in Zagreb and eventually to UN headquarters in New York, where policy-makers were making profound decisions. So anything that was given had to be verified as much as reasonably practical and be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when you say that it had to be verified, can you tell us a little bit about the process by which you went through to verify information?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Normally incidents were investigated by two UNMOs, different nationalities. Every team was made up of a selection of nationalities so there could never be a national bias within a team and incidents were always as much as possible physically verified. For instance, if there was an injury to a person or a claim of an injury, we would go and almost examine the wound, as I had expressed an experience of doing, to make sure that what you were reporting was -- had occurred and was accurately reported on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And was your relationship with either of the parties biased towards one or the other?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In regard to your reporting system, did you have access to other military observers' reports?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: When I worked in the UN headquarters in the UNMO headquarters in the PTT building, yes, I would have been receiving reports from all the other teams. That was in the latter part of my service in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's focus for this moment for the period of time when you were a military observer moving around. During that period of time --

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: In team Zulu?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you have access?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 09390, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now I understand for Mr. Karadzic you had reviewed a map. It was a map of the area south of Sarajevo - and that was 1D04832, it now has a D number. I also understand that that map was a little bit blurry and it was a bit difficult. So thank you for meeting with me yesterday in order to go over a few more points and a new map, and this is one that I showed you with the hopes that we could do away with the ambiguity of the older map. Do you recognise this map?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: The scale is small but it's the general map of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is this the map I showed you yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: It appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And as you saw it yesterday, was it a fair and accurate representation of what you remembered the city of Sarajevo to --

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yeah, it showed -- the location -- the main feature being the river running through and the road that ran parallel to the river and the hill feature where OP 1 was located.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 23917, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, when you and I spoke yesterday, we took this map, which was a much bigger version, I had you make some markings on it so we could see very clearly where, for example, your command post was. Now, we have that map in front of us now -- or do you recognise what's on the screen?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So we see a triangle sort of in the lower half of the map.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What does that represent?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: That is it is best recollection or -- that I can place on the location of OP 1. It was on a prominent hill feature overlooking the city and then a transit line through the brewery towards Sedrenik. So I think, you know, based on a reasonable map reading that that's the approximate location of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now in your statement at paragraph 11 you mentioned that there was a shed nearby that post. What was the shed used for?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: The shed I think was a shepherd's store room. We used it for storing sand for -- we were still working on the OP. Subsidence had occurred and it was beginning to fall down the hill, so it was just an -- fixing it basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: How close was the shed to the OP?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: It was immediate proximity. It was 2, 3 metres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can zoom in further.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Further, further.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We also see -- let me back up. You mentioned in your statement that there was a Bosnian army mortar position that you saw in December 1995 or January 1996. Yesterday you and I spoke about that. Is that the ovalish red circle we see on this map?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yeah, that's my best estimation and -- it was on the road which, as I say, ran parallel to the river. That's the main feature. Now I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And the small red circle north of that oval, that represents the location of the Markale market shelling on the 28th; right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: That's -- you marked that yourself?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do you agree that that approximately represents where it was located?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: The market?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The little red circle.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: You marked that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But my question to you is: Do you agree that that's where it was located?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: The market?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: It was in that general area. There was a plaza. If you look to the north-west of my oval area, I recall that being an open area, and that was the general area where I had seen the impacts, but that was based on my understanding of the topography of the city at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So for the purposes of today, yesterday you also did a measurement from that little small circle to your oval circle, and you did it at about 170 degrees bearing. Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: From the market-place through the mortar positions --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: -- we worked out it's about 170 degrees. Yeah. True. True.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And the distance that you came to between the two was about 500 metres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So just a few minutes ago when Mr. Karadzic was speaking and before he asked you some questions he gave a summary of your statement. And in his -- transcript page 58 today, and he said: "This location," meaning your oval circle, "is in the direction in which it is alleged that the shell had landed in the Markale market it had come from." And that particular sentence, that's not in your statement, is it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yeah. Let's go exactly back to that. It's page 58 today, and the statement made --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please quote me exactly because those weren't my words.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'll read straight from the transcript. "This location is in the direction in which it is alleged that the shell had landed that landed in the Markale market had come from."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That particular sentence that I just read out to you, that's nowhere in your statement, is it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think I made any allegations -- I was just -- any reports I've said are just fact and what I've seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that both maps be tendered, the original base map and this excerpt. And the reason I'm asking for the base map is because it will be used again by me with another witness and I suspect it will be used several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has it not been tendered yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, the original base map, the entire map itself, I don't believe it's ever been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any objections, but there is something missing here. We don't have the direction of approach of the shell. The 170-degree bearing hasn't been marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it may be a subject for your re-examination. We'll give both versions of map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter number 03390 [sic] will be Exhibit P5926, and 65 ter number 23917 will be Exhibit P5927.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And just for the record, I think at line 7 the original 65 ter number is 09390, but I appreciate the new exhibit number. May we have P01957, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Conway, we're about -- on the screen in front of you you're about to see a photo, and I'm going to ask if you recognise this photo. What do you see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: This is the photo which you showed me yesterday. It was more clear in paper form than screen form, so it's a little bit from memory. But I can recognise Harry Konings is our team leader in the foreground to the left, and then it gives you the western view from the O -- from the observation post. There was also an excellent view towards the north and the east, but that would be largely the view we had over the city towards the east.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And so your view from OP 1 was to the -- in the front to the west, to the north, and to the east; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: East, north, and west, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And suffice to say, it was a very good view of the entire city?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: It was an excellent view of that part of the city. That's why the OP was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraph 12 of your report you said that around 11.00 you heard several explosions that were muffled. Can you tell us today what you mean by the term "muffled."

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: It's a -- in relative to an impact explosion which at that distance I would have expected to hear a larger and more -- perhaps the vibration from an impact. At that time it didn't occur to me that the explosions had occurred so close to the OP. It's always something that surprised me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when we spoke about this yesterday you said they were muffled and you thought they were not coming from within your team area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: As you mentioned also in paragraph 12 you said that you had heard several explosions in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now after this day, after this event, you came to understand that there was more than one explosion in the city centre that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And there were, in fact, a total of five explosions at about the time that you speak and the Trial Chamber has heard --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's leading. [In English] Sorry, sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: You are entitled to, so this is your cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has heard evidence about this very exact time of which you speak. They've heard evidence that the timing of the shells, one was at 10.50 in the morning, another at 10.50 in the morning, another at 11.00, another at 11.00, and then one at about 11.14. So my question for you is: Does this timing -- is this timing fairly consistent with the muffled explosions you heard at about 11.00 that day?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: From my memory, if you hadn't given me those times I would have said that the time-span was much closer --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: -- than those times.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You also understand now that the first four shells that landed that day landed in a separate distance a little bit of a ways from the fifth shell that land in front of the Markale market, killing several people. Do you understand that now or after the fact?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Only because you're telling me. At the time when I observed, I saw several plumes of smoke, all reasonably equal in size and shape, which indicated even to me -- even in memory that there was a closer time-span between the shells. So I'm surprised by the times that you're saying to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. A few minutes later after you heard these explosions, you were contacted by UNMO headquarters; right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yeah, and it was quite a short period like it wasn't -- I wouldn't say it was ten minutes, I would say it was within the five-minute bracket.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: How were you contacted?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: On our VHF radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And where you in a place where you could -- was it on your body? Was it in the post? Could you hear it easily?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely where it was, but I always kept the radio within earshot. It was our most important tool on the observation post. So I would have been constantly observing. Even though I was doing the work on the sandbagging, I was constantly observing the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And over the radio you told them that you saw plumes of smoke coming from the market area?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So, Mr. Conway, would you agree with me that the sound of 120-millimetre mortar firing is not - to use your word - muffled if fired from a reasonably close distance to the listener?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: I would expect it to make a very distinctive "vrmph" and "trmph" and you'd know that a heavy explosion had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that sound is not a sound that you heard that morning?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Not what I would have expected from mortars landing so close.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: At the time when this happened you reported that you heard no noise or firing from your area and this remains true today; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Can you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: At the time you reported that you didn't hear any noise or firing from your area; does that remain true today?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean exactly by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I mean in the area around the OP, in the front of the OP, at that time you didn't tell anyone: Oh, I heard a noise coming from that area, did you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: I'll tell you what I saw if that answers your question. I was working. I heard the noises. I didn't think they were so close or in our team area. I received a radio message asking me to confirm that explosions had occurred. I observed over the team area. I saw the plumes of smoke. And I confirmed that impacts had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P01960, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a UNMO patrol report and it's dated from the following day and it's written by Lieutenant-Colonel Konings. You know who he is?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yeah, he was the team leader.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 2 of this exhibit, please. Page 2 of the exhibit. Thank you. And if we can zoom into the middle there is a number 2. That's what I want to focus on. This is the report he wrote and I just want to read this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can do without B/C/S for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe we can make that a little bit bigger.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Great. So under 2A it says: "In the time-frame of the five impacts, UNMOs of" and it looks like it says "ICZ team." Do you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Z I suspect is for team Zulu.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that's your team, right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: "... working on OP-1" then there's a word I can't read, then another word, but then it says: " ... heard no outgoing mortar rounds neither from the Bosnian army territory (general area Bistrik and Colina Kapa) nor from Bosnian Serb army territory." Mr. Conway, is this fact true?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: I can only say that I heard sounds which sounded like impact. I can say -- and I was always confused as had I heard outgoing or incoming. So I can't say that I only heard impact. I don't -- to be honest, I don't know what the explosions I heard were coming from.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But you just said I can only say that I heard sounds which sounded like impact --

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Well I'm using the word -- maybe that's because I know there were impacts, thus I'm saying they're impacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: But like, if someone said, what were those noise -- this was a discussion we had at the time in the team, had you heard outgoing or incoming, and I've never been able to say exactly I'd heard. Since then they've generally been referred to as impacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But nonetheless you also very clearly described the sound that you did hear as muffled, correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And had you heard something closer to your OP in front of your OP, you would not have expected that noise if it were an outgoing 120-millimetre shell -- excuse me, mortar, to be muffled, would you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Can you give me that question again, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Yesterday when we spoke to you, you said that: "I would have thought that outgoing rounds would be louder since a launch point would be only 2 or 3 kilometres away downhill." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: I think you might have misunderstood. I thought that the impacts would have been louder because of the distance from the OP.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 15 of your statement you said: "I would not agree with the proposition that if someone at OP 1 had not heard the sound of outgoing mortar fire, then the fire must have come from the Bosnian Serb side of the confrontation line." That's in your statement. Now it -- I just want to be clear. You disagree with that inference or that conclusion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: I think that in order to make a final analysis on this type of situation you need lots of information from lots of different areas, and to make it on just one piece of information I think is a weak final -- way to make a final analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So that -- but that's one piece of information?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You understand that there were lots of other pieces of information as well?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And pieces of information to which you were not necessarily privy?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Right. You mentioned in your statement at paragraph 17 that there was a Bosnian army mortar position at the bottom of a steep hollow in the southern hills of Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And we spoke about that earlier because you made a marking for me on a chart. You later made a correction that it wasn't the northern side of the road, it was the southern side of the road. You also said in paragraph 22 that the mortar position was well sandbagged. Were sandbags something that were used at the time to prop-up both permanent mortar positions and temporary mortar positions?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by the question, but sandbagging would be a normal military way of giving defence around any type of military installation against incoming fire or shrapnel. Sandbagging takes some time to do. It can be done quite quickly by well-organised military people, but -- so does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It does, thank you. At paragraph 21 you said that the four mortars that you saw there were pointed north towards -- towards Sarajevo. And yesterday you described that a little bit better for me. Can you tell us what exactly you mean by pointing north over -- to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: They were pointing towards the area of, for instance, towards Sedrenik which was on the other side of the confrontation line. They were in a very -- what we call in the military reverse slope position, where the ground behind was rising steeply, and they were in a hollow which was not a manmade hollow. It was more of a natural -- small natural feature, like a mini-quarry type situation. So it was a good military position, I'd have to say, from a military perspective.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And do you remember that -- you just said Sedrenik, but they were pointed north over the city, correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Over the city. And there was -- well, like north of the city was well within the range of a mortar like that. That didn't come as a surprise.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Now in your conversation with Mr. Karadzic on Monday, you noted that during your time at the OP 1 in 1995 you did not observe any mortars required into the city from Serb positions south of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yeah, but I just want -- maybe I need to give some clarity on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Because there had been some firing into the Egyptian Battalion area which was to the north around the area of the river, the library, and then towards the east, and there had been a mortar firing incident at some point while I was there. I can't remember the dates of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now let's talk exactly about the dates. Now, you arrive in Sarajevo about a week before your posting --

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: It's around a week. I arrived on the exact date as the date that there had been an incident on Mount Igman, when there had been an American negotiating team who were leaving the city, and I understand their APC toppled over, it was a French APC, and I think the occupants sadly were killed during that incident. But that marks the date of the arrival.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if I represented to you that that date was August 19th, does that make sense to you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: If that's the date of that, that's the date I arrived in the city, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And then in late September you changed posts -- I shouldn't use the word "post." You changed roles; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: It would have been late September/early October I moved to -- I think I started as duty officer in the UNMO headquarters in PTT, that's the headquarters building.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And from late September through December did your job remain at the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: It did. I was the information officer which -- I was deputy information officer and then information officer which meant I was familiar with both of the teams in the city and the other UNMO teams which were also around other locations in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so that means from August 19th until late September for about those five or six weeks, that's the period of time when you're actually patrolling the city; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Patrolling the city on a daily basis, but also as information officer I would have had to visit teams from time to time and familiarisation with the general terrain.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's focus in on that period of time for those six weeks regarding about how many times you would have been posted at OP 1.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: There were I think about eight UNMOs in the team and we did 48-hour tours of duty on the OP. So the tour of duty of two days came up every four -- once a little bit over every week, so it's about every eight days or so we would have had to do two days on the OP.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So that means during that period of time you were on the OP maybe five to six times?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Mathematically it would seem, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So in answer to Mr. Karadzic's question that there were no mortars fired from the city -- fired into the city from the south while you were at OP 1, it's limited to those five or six times?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yes, but I would have general knowledge -- it was in our immediate team area so if anything happened in the team area most of the team knew what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Let's put aside mortars for the moment. Were there other types of projectiles that were fired into the city of Sarajevo from August to December of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: There were reasonably common occurrences of rocket fire and rifle fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you ever experience sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Once -- I did several times, twice I can think of straight away. Once on my way to PTT from the Sedrenik where we were going down the infamous sniper ally roof and rounds landed around the vehicle on the road, and also in our team based in Sedrenik it was overlooked by a position called sharp stone and from time to time rounds were fired on to the wall of the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is all in the period between August and December of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Closer, August and the end of September, early October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 23904, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, this is going to be a document that's dated September 1st, so this is a period of time where you've not yet changed your position. It's a daily sitrep. You're familiar with this - correct? - or this type of document; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we go to page 17 , please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In the format --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel and witness both slow down for the purpose of interpretation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're only seeing one page at the moment of this, but the format of these sitreps, was this something with which you became familiar?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: I was familiar, yeah, and this would have been -- nothing jumps out as familiar on that particular document, but it was the -- each day we submitted summary reports to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So here we have under 2: "Warring faction movement/observations/investigations." And then we have the "Federation Side." And here it says: "On August 30th, one mortar round impacted inside the Tito Barracks inside the Ukrainian Battalion compound and three mortar artillery rounds impacted outside the Tito barracks." Were you familiar of the location of the Tito barracks?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: I can't remember the names of all the barracks but there were several large barracks in Sarajevo. As I mentioned, there was the Egyptian barracks in our own area and I remember visiting larger barracks where Ukrainian and I think Pakistani barracks were located.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you a map again. May I again have 65 ter number 23917. I know it has an exhibit number now, but 23917.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The date -- can I --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Just an observation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Is that date the 29th of August?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This says on the 30th of August?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: On the 30th because at that time I could still have been on the OP.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And this says it's 120-millimetre mortar from 160 degree bearing. So if we can look at the map again and if we could zoom in, please. And one -- maybe one more, and one more. Now, you see your oval and if you go sort of north-west, there is a big block. Do you recognise that as a barracks -- as the Tito barracks?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yes, I see there -- the block you mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: I recognise that there were barracks in that area. I wouldn't -- if you would just give me a plain map, I wouldn't have found it, but I know there were barracks in that general area.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's fine for now. For the purposes of this question, can you tell me if the document we just looked at said that there was a mortar round coming in at a 160-degree bearing, where would that be coming from then?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: From 160 -- well, 160 is south-east of that position, so it's between -- it probably would be to the south of the marked area, slightly to the south.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So you can actually - if this is enabled - write on the screen, if I could ask for the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you fine with the zooming conditions? Would you like to zoom in further --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Maybe --

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: No, that's enough. I can see clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I draw with this? Well, that's 90 degrees, that's 180. So 30 degrees off that is probably somewhere down -- somewhere down this way. And that's probably -- but that's 45, so 90 and 45 is 135 --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: -- so it's further to -- it's further south, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yeah. So we said 160.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: 160 would be about the second line, this line here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And if you extend that line that you just drew -- oh, that goes into SRK territory, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: It does, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, you just put a little check mark. Can you star that so when we're later looking at this we know which line you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: The checked mark is the correct mark.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Neither mark is [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or for clarity the witness can write down 160.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And now could you sign it, please. Just sign your name on it and date it, and today is the 17th.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: October, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be saved and admitted as the next Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5928, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we go back to 65 ter 23904, please. And may I have page 15. Mr. Conway, earlier you spoke about UNMOs' impartiality, and I want to speak a little bit more about this. In looking at this sitrep report on page 15 - and I want to make sure I said the right number, 23904, yeah, thank you - page 15, under G, can you see this? It says "Military Activity."

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And then we have another column -- columns, observed from, type of fire, origin of fire, impact area. This type of information in this column form, is this something that was typical for UNMO reporting?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: It would have been. Yeah, I'm just looking at it as you speak. Date, time, observed from, type of fire, origin, impact area, remarks, yeah, that's fairly standard stuff, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And under the column of origin of fire we have Jewish cemetery, then unknown, unknown, unknown, and then we have Debelo Brdo, and my apologies for mispronouncing it. Of those two locations that we know, were those Bosnian Serb positions or Bosnian Muslim locations?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: I can't remember the locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Let's go to the next page, 16. And that same column we see sharpstone; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: On the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And was that a Bosnian Serb position?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Sharpstone was Serb position.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we go to the following page, back to page 17, and on the top we see Rajlovac, and then underneath it says BSA BiH. Do you have any memory as to whether this was a Bosnian Serb position or Bosnian Muslim position or both?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: I don't have any recollection. The name doesn't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But is it fair to say that the UNMOs informed their superiors of firing by both the Bosnian Serb side and the Bosnian Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5929, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Conway, yesterday in this courtroom a statement was made, and I'm going to tell you what the statement was and then I'm going to ask you a question about it. The statement that was made was this: "Many UNMO observers were partial to the Bosnian Muslim side and they informed only about the incoming fire but not about the outgoing fire by the Bosnian Muslims, thereby portraying the fighting in Sarajevo as a Serb aggression and shelling." My question for you is: Was this a practice you employed while you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Absolutely no. I would be very proud of the impartiality and accuracy of the UNMO -- all the UNMO officers and the way we operated in Sarajevo and later on in other parts of Yugoslavia, former Yugoslavia too.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do you find the statement that I just read out to be accurate?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: No, no, not at all. It's asserting im -- that the UNMOs weren't impartial. Absolutely no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Just indulgence few minutes, please, to consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I show you two documents, General, did you see any reports outside the period when you were at OP 1? Did you see any reports showing that from that direction there were shells flying over OP 1, not only that week but outside of that period?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: Not while I was in team Zulu can I recall that I heard or any of the other UNMOs speaking of rounds actually going over OP 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now call up in e-court 1D20274.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a sitrep, isn't it, dated June 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't need the Serbian version. Could we now see page 16. Page 16, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it has so many pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D28180 is, in fact, the document I want. Maybe I got the wrong page number for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is also a sitrep dated 19 June 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 7, please. I would like now to read this. [In English] At 18 2300B 1X APC fired by RPG when it coming back from Igman at 19 1615B, numerous shells from down-town (Tito barracks to Poline. At 18th 1615, after Bosnians fired from Tito barracks to BSA side, Serbs fired from Poline to Hotonj with tanks, M18, and mortars. [Interpretation] General, the Marsal Tito barracks was mentioned today. Were you aware of the fact that the Marsal Tito barracks was being used by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and there was such firing from the barracks on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: This incident refers to June 1995. I wasn't in Sarajevo at that time so I can't make any comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's not the incident itself I'm interested in, but in the nature of the Marsal Tito barracks location, were you aware of the fact that the ABiH was using it and that fire was also opened from that location?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CONWAY
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any -- of the facts that you were saying there. My only knowledge of that -- of the barracks, any barracks, that I had been to was occupied by UN troops. There were some locations where we visited liaison officers from the Bosnian army, but I was not aware that units were -- if I understand from what you're saying is that they were located side by side with UN, but I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Thank you for having come to testify here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Unless my colleagues have any questions for you, now you are evidence is concluded. On behalf of this Chamber, I'd like to thank you, General, for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, General.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the following document in the e-court system. Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D6032.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: Is this the statement that we have before us? Would you like to see the last page and the signature?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I can see the first page and that's it.

utterances.text: Was this statement read out to you and does it accurately reflect what you said?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I put the same questions to you today as the questions that are contained in the statement, would your answer be the same?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether I could repeat the very same words, but the substance of my response would be identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to ask you and remind myself too that since we speak the same language we should make brief pauses between question and answer, but I don't have many questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, could this statement be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours 1D6032 will be Exhibit D2331.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the supplementary documents also be admitted into evidence as an integral part of this one, but we could deal with that at the end of the examination-in-chief. I would now like to read out a summary of General Kovacevic's statement. It will be in English in order to be more efficient. [In English] Blagoje Kovacevic held the rank of VRS colonel and currently is an active officer in the armed forces of BH with the rank of brigadier. From May 1992 to October 1992, he was the commander of the Blazuj Brigade in the SRK. Over the following two months he held the position of Chief of Staff of the Rajlovac Brigade from which he was transferred on 9th of December, 1992, to the 1st Sarajevo Motorised Brigade as chief of operations and training. From June 1993 to 1996, he was the commander of the 3rd Infantry Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Motorised Brigade. 99 per cent of the members of his unit were not professional military personnel and he encountered problems achieving effective control. There were no professional snipers in his unit. Blagoje Kovacevic has direct knowledge about the quantity and types of armaments in the Marsal Tito barracks, since he worked as a platoon commander and teaching and conducting training pertaining to some of the weapons available therein. Orders from superior commands were that maximum ammunition savings were to be achieved at all levels. All Muslim units in Sarajevo had the same type of armament as the VRS units, since those were JNA and BH TO weapons. However, Muslim forces were also provided with other types of weapons through various illicit channels. Muslims were militarily organised and armed prior to the outbreak of the conflict in BH/Sarajevo. The Patriotic League in Novi Grad municipality of Sarajevo was set up already in autumn 1991. The order of the Supreme Command was that a decisive defence should be assumed at all attained lines, since there was no interest or need to take areas which were not ethnically defined as Serbian. The objectives of the SRK were, first, not to allow Muslim forces to breakthrough from Sarajevo and be used on the other battle-fields; second, to protect the Serbian population in the area of the city of Sarajevo and its environs; and three, to save as many people as possible who had remained in the city under Muslim control. At all positions where Blagoje Kovacevic had been, not a single offensive action had been executed but exclusively defensive ones. These positions were established at the beginning of the war and they remained unaltered until the end of the war. The lines of disengagement had become closer to one another, due to the Muslim army moving towards Serbian lines by digging communication trenches toward the Serbian positions and by nearing the lines with the assistance of UNPROFOR. Several JNA military facilities in Sarajevo remained in the hands of the Muslim forces, among those -- among others the JNA and Bistrik barracks, the Military Hospital, and the Marsal Tito training centre. Throughout the war Muslims never hid their intentions to provoke incidents which would be reason enough for UNPROFOR or NATO to be deployed on their side. They deliberately opened fire at times of truce to provoke the reaction of the part of the Serb forces so that the latter could then be blamed by -- for causing the incident. The 110th Brigade of the 1st Corps of Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was not a regular unit and in which criminal elements predominantly featured, was known for having publicly promised to take Trebevic and Grbavica and cleanse the city of infidels. At the Kazani execution site situated in the zone of responsibility of that brigade, large number of Serbs from the city were liquidated. Serbs around Sarajevo were arrested and ransom demanded. The mass victims' scenario was often employed since such cases would cause great public outcry, as for instance the Markale incident. He has no information as to who caused these incidents, but sabotage cannot be ruled out. Blagoje Kovacevic believes that the Markale incidents involved the use of explosives as opposed to shells. Main Staff and civilian authorities called for the city to be completely demilitarised and for all heavy weaponry on both sides to be placed under UN control. The Serb side carried that out one-sidedly. In 1992 all PVO weaponry against the air-borne were removed from the vicinity of the Sarajevo airport and at a later stage all 80-millimetres and higher-calibre weapons were removed to a distance to 20 kilometres away from Sarajevo and were controlled by UNPROFOR. All soldiers in the unit were trained in and acquainted with the international law of war and humanitarian law. His unit did not open fire at the civilians and took measures to reduce collateral civilian damages. Orders were passed down to the event -- that in the event of fire opened at civilians, investigations were to be conducted and legally prescribed measures taken against the transgressors. Orders had been given repeatedly by SRK command that fire was to be opened only if lives were directly threatened and then only at targets endangering the security of the unit. He explains that never he or any other members of his unit or their subordinates or superior commands intended to cause civilian casualties, terrorise civilians in the territory under Muslim control, or wield psychological impact on them or attack means of public transportation. They never received or issued any verbal or written orders to that effect. Tram tracks in Sarajevo were about 200 metres behind the Muslim forces. Stray bullets could easily be publicised as deliberate targeting of means of public transportation by Serbian forces. Special Muslim units tried to cut off the Lukavica-Pale road, after which terror against Serbs who had remained in Sarajevo considerably increased. On 6th of January, 1994, Muslim forces executed an attack on the Jewish cemetery and the Vrbanja bridge where a disproportionate high number of civilian casualties occurred. Many positions of adversary unit towered over Grbavica, from where it was under complete control of the opposing units. He also had information that Muslim forces had positions in civilian areas. The entire line of this engagement was in the inhabited areas. Passage of humanitarian convoys was completely unhindered by the Serb forces, whereas abuses for military purposes were committed by the 1st Corps of BH Army as well as the existence of a black market for those supplies in the area of the city under Muslim control. Supply of water, electricity, and gas was never interrupted by the Serb forces, yet Muslim forces would cut off their own supply and attribute it to the Serbian terror.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.text: So you tendered nine exhibits; correct? To be precise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. They will be all admitted and be given numbers in due course. Your cross-examination may start tomorrow, but for that purpose shall we give -- do you think we need to give the witness a warning based upon Rule 90(E) or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think in the future it would be better to give such a warning at the commencement of the witness's testimony not the commencement of cross-examination, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Usually it was the party who draws the attention to those facts, but it just occurred to me right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the time, we'll do that tomorrow. But we'll adjourn today, General, and resume tomorrow at 9.00. But in the meantime, can I remind you that you are not supposed to discuss about your testimony with anybody else. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The hearing is adjourned.
